title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
purpose: It opens the Book of Prayer, gathering transmitted merits of prayer, prohibitions within it, and the doctrine and casuistry of the five appointed prayer times, performance (adā') versus making up (qaḍā'), and the status of one who abandons prayer.

points.text: The author reports Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts as teaching that night prayer benefits the body, earns God's pleasure, opens one to mercy and conforms one to prophetic character, and that one must not pray in laziness or drowsiness, must limit wandering thought (receiving only as much of the prayer as one attended to), and must not look aside, since God says 'I am better for you than that toward which you have turned.'

Also from Ali: prayer is the offering (qurbān) of every godfearing person, no deed is more beloved to God than prayer, and worldly affairs must not distract from its appointed times — God having reproached those 'neglectful of their prayer' (Q 107), meaning heedless of it.

The author cites riddle-questions from a book of legal questions: the man for whom prayer is impermissible yet inexcusable is the one drunk to unconsciousness ('Do not approach prayer while intoxicated'); prayer in a state of purity may still be invalid if performed behind a bedouin (a'rābī), since bedouins are harder in disbelief and hypocrisy and it is impermissible to pray behind them; and an obligatory prayer without bowing or prostration is that of a swimmer unable to reach dry land.

The governing distinction throughout the question-and-answer material is between adā' (prayer performed within its appointed time) and qaḍā' (making up after the time has passed), applied separately to the obligatory prayer, its sunnah, and its optional (nāfilah) prayer.

Responsa rule that missed prayers (fawā'it) take precedence over the current prayer if time remains — one sins by neglecting them — that the sunnah's time is before the obligatory prayer except in Maghrib, whose sunnah is prayed as adā' after the obligatory prayer provided nothing separates them, and that one arriving while the imam prays 'Asr during the Dhuhr time intends Dhuhr with him if Dhuhr's time still holds.

Making up missed prayers or praying voluntarily at sunrise, at the sun's meridian standing, and at sunset is disliked (makrūh), on Friday and other days alike; and the reports record agreement that there is no prayer after Fajr until the sun declines except for making up or obligatory prayers (the consecration prayer, the two rakahs of circumambulation, the two festival prayers and the like), with Friday excepted on the ground that 'the fires are not stoked on it.'

The author holds that one who abandons the prescribed prayers for a long period without excuse is not counted a Muslim during that period and has no deed accepted — citing the Prophet's 'There is nothing between the servant and disbelief except the abandonment of prayer' and Ali's 'Prayer is the pillar of religion' and 'There is no share in Islam for one who abandons prayer.'

The author expressly qualifies this 'disbelief': it means only that nothing is accepted from him since he stands in a disbeliever's position — he is not subject to the poll tax, killing, enslavement of offspring, ritual impurity, or prohibition of his slaughtered meat, because the two testimonies place him within the rulings of Islam.

Upon sincere repentance (tawbah naṣūḥ, Q 66:8, whose 'you who believe' the author glosses as those affirming the two testimonies) God accepts him, he becomes truly a Muslim with all lawful deeds accepted, and he is not required to make up the prayers missed before repentance — though doing so is rewarded — whereas deliberately broken Ramadan fasts from that period must be made up with expiation.

The author reports, from questions of Sulayman ibn Hasan answered by Dawud ibn Ajab, the same ruling: one who cut himself off from prayer and cannot reckon what he missed bears no guilt for the past if he repents sincerely and enters the noble covenant and does not lapse again — and from Muhammad ibn al-Fahd ibn Salah's epistle, that a bequest paid for making up a dead person's prayers is applied in order (obligatory portions, then shaf' and witr, then sunan), prayer taking precedence over the obligatory fast.

In the same epistle the case of the boy who killed his mother before puberty is answered: he should undertake her release and discharge as known in the books of the friends of God, and convey good deeds to her — above all Hajj, since Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq told a wealthy questioner that charity equal to the weight of Mount Abu Qubays would not attain the reward of Hajj — but if she was not a believer or did not pray, he must make up her prayer as far as he is able, since prayer is the first deed God examines.

Al-Qadi al-Nu'man ibn Muhammad, in the book of the interpretation of the Sharia, defines the five prayer times as hidden and known only by indications (Dhuhr when a thing's shadow equals its length, 'Asr when double, Maghrib at the setting of the disc, Isha' al-Akhirah at the vanishing of the white twilight, Fajr from daybreak to near sunrise), so that ten things are present each day and night — five outward prayers and five inward times.

Al-Nu'man further sets prayer's four boundaries, like a house's — the time, the qibla, the wudu, the intention — and its seven obligatory elements: takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, glorification, tashahhud, and the sealing.

Al-Nu'man reports Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah's answer that the Fajr prayer belongs neither to night nor day — for if to night the faster could eat at its time, and if to day its recitation would not be aloud — since two prayers belong to the day's portion, two to the night's, and one stands midway, this being 'the far-reaching wisdom.'

Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inward Nursing, prescribes the witr as three units reciting al-A'la, al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas respectively with the standing qunut after bowing, followed after a separation by two seated units reciting al-Falaq and al-Nas, and identifies the dawn prayer — four units, two voluntary and two obligatory, containing the qunut — as the 'middle prayer' of Q 2:238.

The author closes with Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim's answer (sent from Yemen to Hind in 1145 AH to Muhammad 'Ali ibn Salih al-Badri) that making up prayer follows the rule of fasting — only men make it up on behalf of men — while an aged man too weak to make up prayer prays what he can, another makes up on his behalf, and expiation is made.
